analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for FDA to reject brand-name drug maker petitions that delay cheaper generics.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee on a voice vote in November 2019 but was never taken up by the full committee, never got a floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies can file petitions asking the FDA to delay approval of competing generic drugs; current law lets the FDA deny petitions filed mainly to delay, but the test is vague. The bill lists specific warning signs of a delay-focused petition (such as serial filings, filings with no supporting data, and filings timed near a patent's expiration), lets the FDA deny those petitions, requires a 60-day filing deadline, and sends delay-for-delay's-sake petitioners to the Federal Trade Commission. The practical effect is that cheap generic copies of expensive brand-name drugs would reach patients sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need expensive brand-name medications, since cheaper generic versions of those drugs would become available months or years sooner. Insurers and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid also pay less when generics compete.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high brand-name drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the FDA a concrete list of factors for spotting petitions filed mainly to delay generic approval, including serial petitions, petitions with no supporting data, and petitions timed close to a patent's expiration [S2][S3].
It requires petitioners to file within 60 days of learning the information their petition is based on, closing the door on last-minute filings timed to hold up a competing drug's approval [S2][S3].

If the FDA finds a petition was filed primarily to delay approval, it must refer the petitioner to the Federal Trade Commission, adding a real consequence to a tactic that now carries little risk [S3].

The bill requires the FDA to report to Congress on each petition, the time and resources it consumed, and the estimated delay it caused in approving a competing application, creating public accountability for the tactic [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies, which would lose one of their longest-running tools for keeping generic competitors off the market and preserving monopoly prices. The FDA would also bear some cost in applying the new factors and preparing the required reports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug companies and the FDA

drawbacks.text: Citizen petitions are also a legitimate channel for raising real safety and scientific concerns about a pending drug approval; stricter factors, a 60-day filing deadline, and a referral to antitrust enforcers could discourage petitions that raise genuine issues, even inadvertently [S3].
The bill gives the FDA discretion in weighing the delay factors through guidance, so its effectiveness depends on how aggressively the agency chooses to apply them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients from earlier generic competition is concrete and well-documented as a cost of the current petition process, while the main drawback is a possible chilling effect on legitimate petitions, which the bill mitigates by targeting only petitions whose primary purpose is delay. The design is reasonably targeted, though it leaves a lot to FDA discretion.

outcome.mechanism: It got as far as a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee, which approved it by voice vote in November 2019, but the full committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Levin (D-MI) introduced the bill on April 29, 2019, joined by Rep. Francis Rooney (R-FL), and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S3].
It drew 11 cosponsors — 10 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
The Health Subcommittee held a mark-up session on November 13, 2019, and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote [S5].
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never took further action, and the bill received no House floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to file petitions that delay generic competitors' approval, and with it, monopoly prices for longer. Patients who would have had cheaper generics sooner are worse off.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Companies that use citizen petitions to delay generic competition
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on the petition process, which the industry has long relied on to slow generic approvals

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and a Republican original cosponsor, drew cosponsors from both parties (10 D, 1 R), and cleared the subcommittee on a voice vote; its death had no recorded partisan vote against it.

industries.note: The bill targets the sham-petition tactic brand-name companies use to hold up generic approvals, which keeps their monopoly prices in place for months or years. Their loss is patients' gain, since generics typically cost far less.
With delay petitions more easily denied, generic companies can bring their lower-priced versions to market sooner. Their interest in faster approvals matches patients' interest in cheaper drugs.
